body_html:
Disagreeing politely in Spanish is a skill that makes you sound fluent and confident. Spanish-speaking conversations are often lively, with people interrupting, debating and expressing strong opinions, but there are also many ways to soften disagreement so that it stays friendly. Whether you’re in a meeting, at a family dinner or chatting with friends, these phrases will help you say what you think without sounding rude.

Key takeaways
  • The basic phrase is No estoy de acuerdo (not no estoy acuerdo).
  • Soften with No sé, pero…, Yo lo veo de otra manera.
  • Partial agreement works well: Tienes razón en parte, pero…
  • Lively debate is normal in many Spanish-speaking cultures.
{{toc}}

Disagreeing politely in Spanish: the key phrases

SpanishEnglishStrength
No estoy de acuerdo.I don’t agree.Direct
No estoy del todo de acuerdo.I don’t completely agree.Softer
Yo lo veo de otra manera.I see it differently.Soft
No sé si estoy de acuerdo.I’m not sure I agree.Very soft
Entiendo lo que dices, pero…I understand what you’re saying, but…Diplomatic
¡Qué va!No way! / Not at all!Informal, strong

The RAE dictionary lists estar de acuerdo as the standard expression for agreeing, which is why its negative is the core of polite disagreement.

Partial agreement

Agreeing with part of an argument before disagreeing is the most diplomatic approach:

  • Tienes razón en parte, pero… You’re partly right, but…
  • Es verdad que…, aunque… It’s true that…, although…
  • Puede ser, pero también hay que pensar en… Maybe, but we also have to think about…
  • Sí, pero por otro lado… Yes, but on the other hand…

Choosing between pero and sino matters here; see {{link:pero-vs-sino|pero vs sino}}.

Softening your opinion

  • A lo mejor me equivoco, pero… Maybe I’m wrong, but…
  • Desde mi punto de vista… From my point of view…
  • Yo no lo tengo tan claro. I’m not so sure.
  • No creo que sea buena idea. I don’t think it’s a good idea. (subjunctive after no creo que)
  • ¿Y si lo hacemos de otra forma? What if we do it another way?
{{image:2}}

Disagreeing at work

At work, combine respect with a constructive suggestion. Useful patterns: Entiendo tu postura, pero me preocupa que… (I understand your position, but I’m worried that…), Propongo que lo pensemos un poco más (I suggest we think about it a bit more), ¿Podríamos valorar otra opción? (Could we consider another option?). With managers and clients, especially in Latin America, use usted and more softeners. In Spain, colleagues tend to be more direct, and open disagreement in meetings is common and not seen as rude. See {{link:talking-to-coworkers-in-spanish|talking to coworkers in Spanish}}.

{{book:the-mind-lies}}

Disagreeing with friends and family

  • ¡Qué dices! What are you talking about! (playful)
  • Ni de broma. No way, not even as a joke.
  • Eso no es así. That’s not how it is.
  • Bueno, cada uno tiene su opinión. Well, everyone has their own opinion.
  • Vamos a dejarlo aquí. Let’s leave it there.

Family dinners can get heated over politics or soccer; often the debate is part of the fun. If things get tense, Bueno, ¿cambiamos de tema? (Shall we change the subject?) is a graceful exit. More in {{link:family-dinner-spanish-phrases|family dinner Spanish phrases}}.

Agreeing, too

To balance the conversation: Estoy de acuerdo, Tienes toda la razón, Exacto, Totalmente, Eso es.

A sample conversation

  • A: Creo que deberíamos lanzar el producto en enero. (I think we should launch the product in January.)
  • B: Entiendo lo que dices, pero no estoy del todo de acuerdo. En enero la gente gasta menos. (I understand, but I don’t completely agree. People spend less in January.)
  • A: Tienes razón en parte. ¿Qué propones? (You’re partly right. What do you suggest?)
  • B: ¿Y si lo lanzamos en marzo? (What if we launch it in March?)

Interrupting politely

Spanish conversations often overlap, and waiting for a perfect pause may mean you never speak. Polite ways to jump in include Perdona que te interrumpa, pero… (Sorry to interrupt, but…), Un momento, si me permites… (One moment, if you’ll allow me…) and Déjame decir una cosa (Let me say one thing). If someone interrupts you, Déjame terminar, por favor (Let me finish, please) is polite and firm.

Cultural notes

In Spain and many Latin American countries, debate is a form of engagement, not hostility. People may raise their voices, interrupt and argue passionately, then hug and order another round. Learners sometimes read this as conflict when it’s simply enthusiasm. At the same time, in more hierarchical workplaces, especially in parts of Latin America, openly contradicting a boss in front of others can be awkward; it’s often better to raise concerns privately: ¿Tienes un momento? Quería comentarte una cosa sobre la propuesta.

And when you change your mind, say so gracefully: Está bien, me convenciste (Okay, you’ve convinced me) or Tienes razón, no lo había pensado así.

Final thoughts

Disagree with No estoy de acuerdo, soften with partial agreement and personal framing, and suggest alternatives. In Spanish, a respectful debate can bring people closer. For more everyday situations, see {{link:spanish-phrases-for-everyday-situations|my guide to Spanish phrases for everyday situations}}.

faq.q: How do you say “I disagree” in Spanish?
faq.a: No estoy de acuerdo. For a softer version: No estoy del todo de acuerdo or Yo lo veo de otra manera.

faq.q: How do you disagree politely at work in Spanish?
faq.a: Entiendo tu postura, pero…, ¿Podríamos valorar otra opción? or Propongo que lo pensemos un poco más.

faq.q: Is it no estoy de acuerdo or no soy de acuerdo?
faq.a: No estoy de acuerdo. The expression always uses estar and de.
